title: Meta Global BGP + DNS Outage — Backbone Self-Disconnection Takes Facebook, Instagram & WhatsApp Offline Worldwide
dcName: Facebook Global Backbone / Authoritative DNS (Santa Clara data center recovery site)

severity.usersAffected: All users of Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, Mapillary and Oculus globally (family of apps served the same withdrawn authoritative DNS); precise user count not verified in primary sources
severity.impactUsd: Not verified in primary Meta or Cloudflare sources; widely-cited revenue/market-cap figures remain unsourced and are excluded here
severity.tier: SEV-1 / Global total outage (characterized by CNBC as Facebook's worst outage since 2008)

brief: On 4 October 2021 a single command issued during routine backbone maintenance — intended only to assess global backbone capacity — unintentionally took down every connection in Facebook's backbone, completely severing all of its data centers from the internet. With the backbone gone, Facebook's DNS-serving locations followed their designed safety behavior and declared themselves unhealthy, withdrawing the BGP route advertisements for the authoritative nameservers. That withdrawal pulled Facebook's DNS off the global internet: recursive resolvers everywhere lost any path to the nameservers, so Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, Mapillary and Oculus all failed simultaneously rather than degrading gracefully. Recovery was slow because primary and out-of-band network access were also down, forcing engineers to travel on-site; the intentionally hardened physical and system security of the facilities made restarting systems difficult, with recovery advancing after a team reached and reset servers at the Santa Clara, California data center. The outage ran roughly six to seven hours (15:39 UTC start to general restoration around 22:50 UTC).

magnitude.note: Blast radius and user impact maxed: every Meta property globally offline at once plus loss of internal tooling and badge access. Duration ~6-7h is severe but bounded. Financial score is a qualitative estimate — CNBC called it the worst outage since 2008 — because specific dollar figures are not verified in the primary sources.

sequenceOfEvents.event: During a routine backbone maintenance job, a command is issued intended only to assess the availability of global backbone capacity.
The command unintentionally takes down all connections in Facebook's backbone network, causing a complete disconnection between the data centers and the internet.

With the backbone removed, DNS-serving locations declare themselves unhealthy and withdraw their BGP route advertisements — the designed safety behavior — pulling the authoritative nameservers off the internet.
Cloudflare externally observes the peak of Facebook's BGP routing changes; third-party recursive resolvers worldwide begin losing any route to Facebook's nameservers.

From Cloudflare's external vantage, facebook.com stops resolving (~15:50 UTC) and Facebook is observed to have stopped announcing the routes to its DNS prefixes (15:58 UTC); Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, Mapillary and Oculus (globally unavailable from ~15:39 UTC per Wikipedia) remain down simultaneously.
Engineers find primary and out-of-band network access are also down, so remote debugging is impossible; teams are dispatched on-site to the data centers.
On-site recovery is slowed by the facilities' intentionally high physical and system security; a team gains access and manually resets servers at the Santa Clara, California data center.
From Cloudflare's external vantage, facebook.com begins resolving again (~21:20 UTC) and reconnection is observed (~21:28 UTC) as backbone routes return.
BGP routing restored for the affected prefixes (Wikipedia internal timeline).
DNS services begin to be available again.
General platform restoration; services return after internal warm-up following route and DNS recovery. Meta confirms services are back online and apologizes.

metrics.label: Historical scale
metrics.value: Worst Facebook outage since 2008 (per CNBC, via Wikipedia)

rootCause: During a routine backbone maintenance job, a single command issued to assess the availability of global backbone capacity unintentionally took down every connection in Facebook's backbone, completely disconnecting all data centers from the internet. This is Meta's own unambiguous statement of cause: a human-issued, insufficiently-guarded maintenance command whose blast radius was the entire backbone rather than a bounded assessment.
contributingFactors: The DNS-serving locations were designed to withdraw their BGP advertisements when they detect they are unhealthy — a safety mechanism that, given a total backbone loss, correctly but catastrophically pulled the authoritative nameservers off the internet.

Facebook's family of apps shared the same authoritative DNS and the same disconnected backbone, so there was no property-level isolation — the failure hit everything at once instead of degrading partially.
Primary and out-of-band network access were both down, eliminating remote recovery and forcing physical on-site intervention.
The data centers' intentionally high physical and system security — a deliberate hardening choice — slowed the very engineers who needed emergency access to restart systems.
The maintenance command lacked an effective guardrail or audit that would have prevented a capacity-assessment action from disabling all backbone connections.

coe.action: Meta published no formal numbered Correction-of-Errors action list. The day-of post confirmed restoration and apologized; the stated corrective direction is a general commitment to strengthen testing, drills and resilience rather than enumerated action items.
coe.status: Stated as general commitment; no enumerated items published

coe.action: Strengthen the auditing and guardrails around backbone maintenance commands so that a capacity-assessment action cannot take down all backbone connections (inferred corrective direction consistent with Meta's stated intent to harden testing and resilience).
coe.status: Directional commitment — not published as a discrete tracked item

coe.action: Improve out-of-band access and physical-recovery readiness so hardened-facility security does not block emergency restarts during a total network loss (inferred from the documented recovery bottleneck).
coe.status: Directional commitment — not published as a discrete tracked item

lessonsLearnt: A safety mechanism (health-based BGP withdrawal) is only as safe as its assumptions: when the 'unhealthy' signal is the loss of the entire backbone, the designed self-protection amplifies a local fault into a global one.
Shared authoritative DNS and a shared backbone across a family of apps remove all fault isolation — a single control-plane event can take down every product at once.

Control-plane dependencies must not gate their own recovery: when the same backbone carries both production traffic and the operators' management/out-of-band access, an outage locks operators out of the fix.
Physical security hardening and emergency-recovery speed are in tension; recovery runbooks must plan for the case where the only path in is a manually secured, deliberately hard-to-enter facility.
Maintenance commands with facility-wide or backbone-wide reach need guardrails and pre-execution auditing proportional to their blast radius, not to their intended (narrow) purpose.
External vantage points (e.g. Cloudflare's BGP/DNS observations) independently corroborated the failure chain, showing the value of third-party visibility when internal telemetry is itself offline.
improvements: Add pre-execution validation and blast-radius auditing to backbone maintenance tooling so a capacity-assessment command cannot disable all backbone connections.
Decouple operator management and out-of-band access from the production backbone so engineers retain a control path during a total data-plane outage.
Introduce isolation between the authoritative DNS / BGP posture of independent properties so a single withdrawal event cannot deplatform the entire app family simultaneously.
Constrain or dampen automated BGP withdrawal so a catastrophic 'all unhealthy' signal triggers escalation rather than an instantaneous global route pull.
Pre-stage on-site emergency-access procedures and personnel at hardened facilities so physical security does not become the recovery bottleneck.
Invest in drills and resilience testing (per Meta's stated direction) that specifically rehearse total-backbone-loss and locked-out-operator scenarios.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Failure mechanism
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: The proximate trigger was a single maintenance command intended only to assess global backbone capacity. Instead of a read-only assessment, it took down every connection in the backbone, producing a complete disconnection between Facebook's data centers and the internet. Because the action hit the backbone as a whole, there was no partial degradation — the data plane simply vanished, which is why the impact was total and instantaneous rather than gradual.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why it cascaded globally
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Facebook's DNS-serving locations are designed to withdraw their BGP route advertisements whenever they judge themselves unhealthy — a normal safety behavior meant to steer traffic away from a bad node. When the entire backbone disappeared, those locations all declared themselves unhealthy at once and withdrew their advertisements, pulling the authoritative nameservers off the internet. Cloudflare, from an external vantage, confirmed the chain: with Facebook no longer announcing its DNS prefix routes via BGP, every recursive resolver worldwide lost any path to the nameservers. A backbone fault thus converted into a global DNS blackout, and because the whole app family shared that DNS, all properties failed together.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Why recovery took hours
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Recovery was slow for a structural reason: primary and out-of-band network access were both down, so remote debugging and remote fixes were impossible. Meta had to send engineers physically on-site. There, the data centers' intentionally high levels of physical and system security — normally a virtue — made it slow to get in and restart systems. The concrete turning point was a team reaching the Santa Clara, California data center and manually resetting servers. The multi-hour duration (start 15:39 UTC, general restoration ~22:50 UTC) is the direct consequence of a control plane that depended on the very network that had failed.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Organizational and systemic factors
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: Several deliberate design and operational choices combined to widen the blast radius: a shared backbone and shared authoritative DNS across independent-seeming products (Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, Mapillary, Oculus) removed fault isolation; management/out-of-band access rode the same infrastructure it was meant to rescue; and hardened facility security had no fast emergency-access path for a total-outage scenario. Notably, Meta published no enumerated Correction-of-Errors list — only a general commitment to strengthen testing, drills and resilience — so the corrective posture is directional rather than trackable.

comprehensiveAnalysis.heading: Cross-incident pattern
comprehensiveAnalysis.body: This outage is a canonical example of a self-inflicted control-plane collapse: a routine change with an unexpectedly large blast radius triggers an automated safety mechanism (BGP withdrawal) that removes the organization's own reachability, after which the same failure blocks the recovery path. The pattern — automation amplifying a human command, shared dependencies collapsing isolation, and operators locked out by their own hardening — recurs across large-scale network outages and argues for blast-radius guardrails, independent management planes, and rehearsed lock-out recovery.

technicalDeepDive: The failure is best understood as a two-stage collapse spanning the data plane and the routing control plane. Stage one: a backbone maintenance command, meant to assess available global backbone capacity, instead disabled all connections in Facebook's backbone, producing a complete disconnection of server connectivity between the data centers and the internet. This is a pure data-plane event, but its magnitude — the entire backbone, not a segment — is what made stage two catastrophic. Stage two is routing-driven: Facebook's authoritative DNS is served from multiple locations that continuously self-assess health and, per design, withdraw their BGP prefix advertisements when they conclude they cannot reach the rest of the network. With the backbone gone, every DNS location simultaneously judged itself unhealthy and withdrew its advertisements, so the prefixes covering Facebook's nameservers were no longer announced to the global routing table. From Cloudflare's external position this was unmistakable: with Facebook no longer announcing its DNS prefix routes through BGP, their and everyone else's resolvers had no way to connect to the nameservers, so every DNS lookup for facebook.com and the sister domains failed at the resolution stage — before any TCP/TLS could even be attempted. The single shared authoritative DNS and shared backbone across the app family meant there was no per-property blast-radius containment, so Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, Mapillary and Oculus went dark together.\n\nThe recovery profile is dictated by dependency inversion in the management plane. Both primary and out-of-band access traversed infrastructure that was itself down, collapsing the normal remote-remediation path and forcing physical dispatch to the data centers. The facilities' hardened physical and system security — designed to keep unauthorized people out — slowed authorized emergency responders, with the concrete recovery instance being a team gaining access to and resetting servers at the Santa Clara data center. Once the backbone and BGP announcements were re-established, restoration was still not instantaneous: external observers (Cloudflare) saw routes and resolution return around 21:20-21:28 UTC, while Meta's internal timeline records BGP restored at ~21:50 UTC, DNS resumed at 22:05 UTC, and general service restoration by ~22:50 UTC. The gap between the external route-return and the internal 'fully restored' marks is best explained as service warm-up — caches, sessions and back-end fleets re-converging after routes and DNS came back — rather than a contradiction between vantage points. No single canonical end-timestamp was published by Meta, and revenue/user-count figures are not verified in the primary sources, so they are excluded from this analysis.
